sources.alt: A black-and-white printed world map made of twelve joined sheets in three rows of four, with Latin captions along the bottom reading 'Universalis cosmographia secundum Ptholomaei traditionem et Americi Vespucii aliorumque lustrationes'; two portraits in the top row face each other beneath Latin labels (a seated figure holding a small globe on the left under the name of Ptolemy, and a standing figure on the right under the name of Americus Vespucius), the large middle sheets show Europe, the Mediterranean, Africa with an elephant, and Asia in detail, and a narrow strip of coastline at the far left edge shows the lands across the Atlantic.
sources.credit: Universalis cosmographia, Martin Waldseemuller, 1507. Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).
sources.notes: The map was printed at Saint-Die in Lorraine and is the earliest known map to use the name America; the western lands appear on a narrow strip at the left edge, and the sheets are shown joined together here.

sources.alt: A color poster printed for the magazine London Opinion: a red box at the top reads 'London Opinion', below it a half-length portrait of a stern man with a large mustache in a white-topped military cap and dark uniform points his gloved finger straight out at the viewer, with the words 'Your country needs YOU' in large letters beside the hand, and '1d London Opinion 1d' in red at the bottom.
